target_feature_label: SDH-deficient GIST (succinate-driven redox stress and a blocked TET demethylation axis)
mechanism: SDH loss drives succinate up, and succinate jams the alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent TET demethylases and prolyl hydroxylases that this tumor's biology runs through. Pharmacologic ascorbate can refuel TET activity by keeping its catalytic iron reduced. At gram-level plasma concentrations it also acts as a pro-oxidant, generating extracellular H2O2 that SDH-deficient cells, already carrying an iron and redox burden, are poorly equipped to mop up.
rationale: In SDHB-low pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma models, pharmacologic ascorbate caused oxidative DNA damage and apoptosis, shrank metastatic lesions in vivo, and extended survival. The upstream lesion that did the work there (SDH loss, then succinate, then a redox and methylation derangement) is exactly what defines this patient's tumor, so the vulnerability has a fair chance of carrying across even though the histology differs. It is off-patent, cheap, and already given IV in solid-tumor trials, just never in SDH-deficient GIST.
novelty: There is no oncology development program or registered trial for ascorbate in SDH-deficient GIST; the supporting work sits in PPGL models, so this is a repurposing hypothesis rather than anything the trial screener would already hold.

key_manuscripts.finding: Pharmacologic ascorbate disrupted redox homeostasis in SDHB-knockdown pheochromocytoma cells, triggering oxidative DNA damage and apoptosis, and in a PCPG allograft model it suppressed SDHB-low metastatic lesions and prolonged survival.

model_systems: SDHB-knockdown MPC and hPheo1 cell lines
developability: An off-patent drug already infused at gram-level doses in existing oncology trials, so a dSDH-GIST window or basket study would be logistically simple to stand up. The real obstacle is commercial: nobody owns it, which is the usual reason high-dose ascorbate stalls before a definitive trial.
risks: The supporting data are in PPGL, not GIST; the redox vulnerability is assumed to transport but has not been shown in dSDH-GIST.
High-dose IV vitamin C carries real toxicity in G6PD deficiency (hemolysis) and a risk of oxalate nephropathy.
Direction of effect is not guaranteed; in some contexts ascorbate is cytoprotective rather than cytotoxic.
caveats: Cross-tumor inference from SDHB-mutant PPGL models. No GIST-specific ascorbate data exist yet.

intervention_label: LDH (LDHA) inhibition with tool compounds (oxamate, GNE-140)
target_feature_label: SDH-deficient GIST (glycolytic NAD+ dependency from a broken TCA cycle)
mechanism: With SDH out, the TCA cycle is broken at complex II and the cell leans on glycolysis to make ATP. That forces a dependency on lactate dehydrogenase to regenerate NAD+ by converting pyruvate to lactate. Block LDHA and the SDH-deficient cell can no longer balance its redox books.
rationale: In an isogenic SDHC-loss model, both LDHA knockdown and the LDH inhibitors oxamate and GNE-140 cut viability preferentially in the SDH-deficient cells, with PC knockdown a weaker hit by comparison. The dependency falls straight out of the metabolic rewiring SDH loss imposes, so it should hold in dSDH-GIST in principle. This is an in-vitro synthetic-lethal signal, not a therapy.
novelty: No selective, clinical-grade LDHA inhibitor exists and there is no trial in any indication; the molecules here are academic tool compounds, well outside the trial screener's scope.

key_manuscripts.finding: An isogenic SDHC-disrupted cell model was selectively vulnerable to LDHA knockdown and to the LDH inhibitors oxamate and GNE-140, identifying NAD+-regenerating glycolysis as a metabolic synthetic-lethal point in SDH-loss cells.

developability: No drug-like, selective LDHA inhibitor has cleared the tox and PK bar for humans. The LDH-inhibitor field has wrestled with potency and selectivity for years, so a real molecule would need to exist before this idea is testable.
risks: LDHA is broadly essential across normal tissues, and tumor-selective killing has not been shown in vivo for SDH-loss models.
Tool compounds like oxamate (low potency) and GNE-140 carry off-target effects that muddy the synthetic-lethal claim.
The model is murine fibroblasts and chromaffin cells, a long way from gastric dSDH-GIST.

intervention_label: Pyruvate carboxylase (PC) dependency as a synthetic-lethal target (no clinical inhibitor yet)
target_feature_label: SDH-deficient GIST (aspartate-pool dependency on pyruvate carboxylation)
mechanism: Because the TCA cycle cannot run forward past complex II, SDH-deficient cells drain their aspartate pool. They refill it by carboxylating pyruvate to oxaloacetate through pyruvate carboxylase, which makes PC an enzyme they cannot do without. Cut off pyruvate carboxylation and aspartate biosynthesis collapses, stalling proliferation.
rationale: Two independent groups showed that Sdh-null cells stall or die when pyruvate carboxylation is blocked genetically, with the dependency confirmed in xenografts and traced directly by stable-isotope labeling. It is one of the cleaner metabolic synthetic-lethal nodes in SDH-loss biology and was explicitly named as a vulnerability for future treatment of SDH-associated cancers. The honest catch: there is no pyruvate carboxylase inhibitor anyone could give a patient.
novelty: Not a drug, not a trial, and absent from every upstream file. This is a validated target with no clinical-grade molecule yet, which is the not-yet-drugged category this scan exists to surface.

key_manuscripts.finding: Sdhb-null cells upregulated pyruvate carboxylase to divert pyruvate into oxaloacetate and sustain aspartate synthesis; blocking this pathway arrested growth, identifying PC as a metabolic vulnerability of SDH-associated malignancy.
Independent isotope-tracing work confirmed that loss of SDH activity makes cells dependent on pyruvate carboxylation to resupply the depleted aspartate pool for anabolism.

developability: No selective PC inhibitor is in development, and PC is widely expressed for gluconeogenesis and anaplerosis, so a tumor-selective therapeutic window is unproven. This reads as a target worth a discovery campaign (small molecule or degrader), not something that can be tested in a patient today.
risks: There is no molecule to give; the candidate is target validation only.
Systemic PC inhibition would risk hypoglycemia and broad metabolic toxicity.
The dependency was shown in kidney and PPGL models, not GIST.
Cells may reroute anaplerosis through glutamine as a resistance escape.
caveats: A target-validation finding, not a therapy. The biology is reproduced and in vivo, but the gap to a usable drug is large.

intervention_label: SSTR2-targeted peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (177Lu-DOTATATE), selected by 68Ga-DOTATATE PET
mechanism: SDH-deficient tumors tend to put somatostatin receptor 2 on the cell surface, the same biology that makes paragangliomas DOTATATE-avid. 177Lu-DOTATATE binds SSTR2 and delivers beta-radiation into the cell. The receptor doubles as both the imaging handle (on 68Ga-DOTATATE PET) and the therapeutic target.
rationale: A metastatic SDHA-mutant GIST with strong SSTR2A staining and DOTATATE-avid disease had a partial response lasting more than a year on 177Lu-DOTATATE after failing imatinib and sunitinib, and a separate SDHB-deficient GIST showed clear Ga-68 DOTATATE avidity. Because the target can be confirmed non-invasively with a PET scan before committing, this is an unusually testable idea for a rare tumor. The radioligand is already approved for neuroendocrine tumors, so dosimetry and manufacturing are settled.
novelty: Approved for gastroenteropancreatic NETs and used off-label in a couple of GIST case reports, but with no registered PRRT trial in GIST. This is a repurposing hypothesis, not a clinical-stage GIST program the trial screener would carry.

key_manuscripts.finding: An SDHA-mutant metastatic GIST with diffuse strong SSTR2A IHC and DOTATATE-avid disease achieved a partial response durable beyond 14 months on four cycles of 177Lu-DOTATATE after progressing on imatinib and sunitinib.

An SDH-deficient (SDHB-negative) KIT/PDGFRA-WT metastatic GIST showed significant somatostatin-receptor avidity on Ga-68 DOTATATE PET, supporting SSTR-directed imaging and PRRT eligibility in selected TKI-resistant patients.

model_systems: human SDH-deficient GIST case reports (SSTR2A IHC, 68Ga-DOTATATE PET)
developability: The radioligand is FDA-approved and PRRT centers already exist, so a dSDH-GIST window or basket gated on DOTATATE-PET positivity is feasible now. What is missing is prospective data and a sponsor willing to run it in such a rare subtype.
risks: SSTR2 expression in dSDH-GIST is documented only at case level, not systematically; it may be heterogeneous or absent in a given patient.
The response evidence is anecdotal (two case reports).
Renal and bone-marrow dosimetry constrain repeat dosing.
This patient is currently NED, with no measurable, PET-confirmable target to treat.
caveats: These are human off-label case reports rather than preclinical data, but with no GIST trial in existence the idea still sits in the horizon-scan gap. Confirm SSTR2 avidity on PET before acting.

intervention_label: GRPR-targeted radioligand therapy (e.g. 177Lu-NeoB / RM2), selected by 68Ga-NeoB PET
target_feature_label: SDH-deficient GIST (cell-surface gastrin-releasing peptide receptor expression)
mechanism: Gastrin-releasing peptide receptor sits on the surface of SDH-deficient wild-type GIST. A GRPR antagonist ligand such as NeoB carries a gallium-68 label for PET and a lutetium-177 label for therapy, so GRPR works as a paired imaging-and-treatment target the way SSTR2 does in neuroendocrine tumors.
rationale: A 2025 imaging study used 68Ga-NeoB PET to show in vivo GRPR expression across SDH-deficient wtGIST lesions and framed it explicitly as patient selection for future GRPR therapeutic trials. GRPR is a surface target independent of SSTR2, so it widens the radioligand options for a subtype with very few drugs. No therapeutic dose has been given to a GIST patient yet; the work stops at imaging.
novelty: GRPR radioligand therapy is in early trials for prostate and breast cancer but has no GIST program, and the dSDH-GIST evidence is an imaging and expression study alone, earlier than anything the trial screener tracks.

key_manuscripts.finding: 68Ga-NeoB PET demonstrated in vivo GRPR expression across lesions in patients with SDH-deficient wild-type GIST, positioning GRPR as a theranostic target and a selection biomarker for future radioligand therapy trials in this subtype.

model_systems: in vivo 68Ga-NeoB PET in SDH-deficient wild-type GIST patients
developability: GRPR-directed 177Lu radioligands (NeoB, RM2) are in clinical development for other tumors, so the therapeutic agent already exists, but the dSDH-GIST work stops at imaging. A therapy trial gated on 68Ga-NeoB PET positivity is the logical next step.
risks: Only expression and imaging data exist in GIST; there are zero therapeutic outcomes to point to.
GRPR levels are likely heterogeneous across lesions and patients.
Physiologic pancreatic GRPR uptake constrains dosimetry.
This patient is NED, with no measurable target to image or treat right now.
caveats: Imaging-stage evidence only. Earlier and less proven than the SSTR2/DOTATATE option, but a genuinely independent target.

intervention_label: Ferroptosis induction (GPX4 or system xc- inhibition)
target_feature_label: SDH-deficient GIST (iron and lipid-peroxidation redox vulnerability)
mechanism: SDH-deficient cells carry an iron and redox burden, and complex II normally helps keep the lipophilic CoQ antioxidant pool reduced. If losing SDH forces a harder reliance on GPX4 and glutathione to hold off membrane lipid peroxidation, then inhibiting GPX4 or the cystine importer system xc- could push these cells over the edge into ferroptosis.
rationale: This is a hypothesis, flagged as a direction rather than a result. The redox-stress angle has real support in SDH-loss models (the same oxidative weakness the ascorbate work exploits), and recent work links the complex II / CoQ axis to ferroptosis defense. But I could not verify any GPX4-inhibitor experiment in SDH-deficient GIST, or even in dSDH-PPGL, so the specific ferroptosis claim is unproven here.
novelty: No drug, no trial, and no GIST-specific data; a mechanistic hypothesis only, which keeps it well clear of the other agents.
developability: Clinical-grade GPX4 inhibitors do not exist yet; the field is still on tool compounds like RSL3 and ML162 that struggle with stability and selectivity. The only repurposable handle is weak system xc- inhibition via sulfasalazine. Mostly this needs target validation in an SDH-deficient model before it is worth more.
risks: Entirely unvalidated in any SDH context.
Direction of effect is genuinely uncertain; in some settings intact SDH supports ferroptosis resistance, so SDH loss could cut either way.
No deliverable GPX4 inhibitor exists.
This may simply be the wrong call.
caveats: I nearly left this out. Kept as a low-priority research direction with no supporting manuscript, not as an actionable idea.

mechanism: With the TCA cycle broken at complex II, SDH-deficient cells lean on glutamine anaplerosis to keep carbon flowing, which makes glutaminase a metabolic dependency. CB-839 blocks glutaminase to starve that route.
rationale: The metabolic logic fits SDH-deficient biology well, and FH/SDH-deficient renal models show GLS1 dependency. But this has already been carried into the clinic in exactly this population.
exclusion_reason: This one already had its turn in the clinic. The CB-839 solid-tumor study NCT02071862 included a Part 2 cohort of SDH-deficient GIST (alongside FH-deficient and other SDH-deficient tumors), so glutaminase inhibition in this exact population is clinical-stage and belongs to the trial screener, not to a forward-looking horizon scan. Note the development_stage field is capped below clinical maturity by the schema; the true status is past first-in-human.

mechanism: EZH2 writes the repressive H3K27me3 mark as the catalytic core of PRC2. The idea was that the SDH-deficient hypermethylator phenotype might create a PRC2 dependency an EZH2 inhibitor could exploit.
rationale: An epigenetic angle is appealing in a tumor defined by a methylation derangement, but the specific EZH2 dependency was not borne out in the literature for this subtype.
exclusion_reason: Two problems. Tazemetostat is approved and heavily trialed (SWI/SNF-altered tumors, follicular lymphoma), so it is clinical-stage and outside this scan. And I found no dSDH-GIST-specific preclinical evidence that PRC2 is the relevant dependency here, so there is no novel, SDH-anchored rationale to carry it as a horizon candidate. The schema caps development_stage below clinical; the true status is approved/in-trial.

mechanism: LSD1/KDM1A demethylates H3K4 and H3K9 marks. It came up as a candidate epigenetic target in a tumor defined by a methylation derangement.
rationale: Considered as an epigenetic-axis option, but the mechanistic link to this patient's SDH biology does not hold up on inspection.
exclusion_reason: Mechanism does not map onto the stated feature. LSD1 is a FAD-dependent demethylase, not an alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent one, so succinate does not directly inhibit it and there is no oncometabolite-driven LSD1 dependency in SDH-deficient tumors that I could find. Several LSD1 inhibitors are also already in trials, putting them outside this scan regardless.
